summary: Defines Encrypted Key Transport (EKT), an extension to DTLS and SRTP for securely carrying SRTP master keys and related information inside SRTP itself. This helps decentralized conferences by letting keys be distributed to many participants. It is standards-track.

eli5.summary: In a group call, everyone needs the same secret key. This document describes a way to pass the key around inside the call's own packets, wrapped in a lock only the group can open.

questions: how to distribute srtp keys in a conference
how does ekt work with dtls-srtp
what is the ekt_key handshake message
subtitle: Carries each sender's SRTP key inside its own packets, wrapped in a group key delivered over DTLS.

tldr.problem: SRTP needs SSRC values, keys and other state coordinated among all participants, which is hard in decentralized or large conferences where a joiner must learn every source's key.
tldr.mechanism: Each sender appends an EKTField to its SRTP packets, holding its SRTP master key, SSRC and rollover counter encrypted under a shared EKTKey. The EKTKey is delivered to each endpoint by a DTLS-SRTP extension.
tldr.outcome: Endpoints can choose SSRCs and keys freely and receivers learn keys from the media stream itself. The cost is that group members share a key, so they cannot authenticate one another.

today: RFC 8870 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2021, and the metadata shows no obsoleting or updating RFC.

sections.title: Why SRTP Needs Help in Groups
sections.content:
RTP is designed for decentralized groups with minimal control, but Secure RTP (SRTP, RFC 3711) needs SSRC values and other data to be coordinated among all participants. A participant who joins late has to be told the SRTP keys, the SSRC and the rollover counter (ROC) of every source.

Encrypted Key Transport (EKT) removes much of that external signaling. Endpoints can pick SSRCs as they like and start new sources with new master keys without coordinating. EKT does not replace key establishment; it works alongside it, and this RFC defines the combination with DTLS-SRTP.
sections.eli5: Normally someone has to hand every new person every other person's secret code. EKT lets the codes travel along with the messages instead.

sections.title: How the Pieces Fit
sections.content:
The DTLS server gives the client an EKTKey during the DTLS handshake. That key encrypts the SRTP master key an endpoint uses for the media it sends, and the encrypted key is sent along with the SRTP packet. Anyone who knows the EKTKey can decrypt the master key and then the media.

The architecture in RFC 8871 uses this: each participant makes a DTLS-SRTP connection to a common Key Distributor, which hands out the same EKTKey to everyone. The RFC says EKT suits conferences where the central Media Distributor cannot decrypt the media, and large conferences where the bridge can decrypt but wants to encrypt once and send the same media to many participants.
sections.eli5: A helper hands everyone the same key to a lockbox. Each person puts their own code in the box and sends it with their messages.

sections.title: The EKTField
sections.content:
An EKTField (an "EKT Tag") is appended at the end of the SRTP packet, after the authentication tag if present. There are two forms. The ShortEKTField is a single zero byte. The FullEKTField holds the EKT ciphertext, a 2-byte Security Parameter Index (SPI), a 2-byte Epoch, a 2-byte length and a final message type byte of 2.

The ciphertext is made by encrypting the EKTPlaintext: the master key length, the master key, the 4-byte SSRC and the 4-byte ROC. The SSRC inside MUST match the SSRC in the SRTP header. The SPI selects the EKTKey, cipher and master salt. The Epoch counts keys already sent for that SSRC under the current EKTKey, and receivers MUST reject a FullEKTField whose epoch is equal to or lower than one already seen. EKT MUST NOT be used with SRTP's MKI or <From, To>. Message type 1 is not available, because legacy implementations used it.
sections.eli5: The tag on the end of each message is either a blank sticker (short) or a sticker with the locked box and a label saying which key opens it (full).

sections.title: Sending and Receiving Packets
sections.content:
A sender with a full tag sets the SPI, builds the EKTPlaintext from the same master key, SSRC and ROC SRTP uses, and encrypts it with the EKTKey. After sending a new key, outbound packets SHOULD keep using the old master key for 250 ms so receivers have time to get the new one.

A receiver looks at the last byte to tell short from full. For a full tag it finds the parameter set by SPI (no match counts as an authentication failure), decrypts and authenticates the ciphertext, and checks that the SSRC matches the packet. It then saves the master key, ROC and salt, indexed by SSRC, and carries on with normal SRTP. Failures abort EKT processing and the receiver SHOULD discard the packet. Receivers MAY try both the old and new key to avoid loss during a rekey, but only if the SRTP transform has integrity protection.
sections.eli5: The receiver peeks at the last bit of the message to see which sticker it is. If it is the full one, they open the box with the group key and learn the sender's code.

sections.title: EKT Ciphers
sections.content:
EKT uses an authenticated cipher with an encryption function E(K, P) and a decryption function D(K, C) that can report an invalid ciphertext. Each cipher has a limit T on how often one key may be used, and an EKTKey MUST NOT be used more than T times. Retransmitting the same FullEKTField counts as one encryption.

The default is AES Key Wrap with Padding (RFC 5649), which MUST be implemented as AESKW128 with a 16-byte key. AESKW256 uses a 32-byte key and MAY be implemented. Both have T of 2^48. New ciphers can be registered, MUST provide integrity protection and define their own L and T.
sections.eli5: The lockbox has to be a good one that notices if someone tampers with it. The RFC picks a standard box and says how many times one key may be used.

sections.title: When to Send Full Tags
sections.content:
Keys travel with the media, so timing matters. A new sender SHOULD send a FullEKTField as soon as possible, ideally in its first packet, and a rekey is announced the same way. In both cases the RFC RECOMMENDS sending the full tag in three consecutive packets to survive loss.

New receivers are unknown to senders, so senders SHOULD periodically send the full tag. With audio and video the RECOMMENDED frequency matches the rate of intra-coded video frames, and with audio only it is every 100 ms. Otherwise a ShortEKTField SHOULD be sent. Sending full tags less often saves bandwidth but slows joins and rekeys.
sections.eli5: New people may show up at any time, so each sender keeps repeating the full box now and then. Sending it more often costs more, but newcomers join faster.

sections.title: EKT in DTLS-SRTP
sections.content:
This RFC adds a TLS extension, supported_ekt_ciphers, and a handshake message, ekt_key (type 26). The client lists its EKT ciphers in preference order in the ClientHello, and the server answers with the chosen one. The server then MUST send the client an EKTKey message holding the key value, an SRTP master salt, a 16-bit ekt_spi and a 24-bit ekt_ttl, the maximum number of seconds the key may be used.

The recipient MUST reply with an ACK, and the EKTKey and ACK follow the retransmission rules of the negotiated DTLS version. An unprocessable EKTKey MUST get a DTLS alert. EKT works with DTLS versions before 1.3 too, but then the ACK needs explicit support. Because the negotiation happens in the DTLS handshake, SDP offer/answer is unchanged. In a multi-party setup, each endpoint handshakes with a central server that sets one common EKTKey, which avoids many pairwise handshakes but stops endpoints from directly authenticating each other.
sections.eli5: When joining, you and the helper agree on which kind of lockbox to use, then the helper passes you the group key and you say thanks (ACK).

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
EKT inherits the security of the key management that sets the EKTKey. Each sender and receiver MUST generate distinct SRTP master keys, and master keys MUST be randomly generated, not reused and not derived from other master keys. The SSRC inside the plaintext stops an attacker pasting one stream's EKT tag onto another, and the Epoch stops rollback to an earlier key.

The RFC lists limits. EKT has no replay protection, and forged full tags can waste receiver CPU. The EKTKey is a group shared symmetric key, so members can impersonate one another and the key distributor can decrypt any media. The EKTKey MUST NOT outlive its TTL, which also bounds how long a blocked rekey message can leave an endpoint on an old key. The EKT cipher key length MUST be at least as long as the SRTP and DTLS-SRTP ciphers.
sections.eli5: Everyone in the group holds the same key, so anyone in the group could pretend to be someone else. The key also has an expiry date so old keys stop working.

fields.name: Security Parameter Index
fields.desc: Selects the EKTKey, cipher and master salt.

fields.name: Epoch
fields.desc: Count of keys already sent for this SSRC under the current EKTKey.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the FullEKTField in octets, including this field and the type.

messages.label: EKTKey
messages.note: Sent under DTLS application traffic keys.
